name: Cusco
info: Cusco is a city in the Andes of south-eastern Peru, at about 3,400 metres, founded in the 12th century according to tradition and for centuries the capital of the Inca Empire.

facts.founded: In the 12th century by Manco Cápac, according to Inca tradition; the Killke people occupied the region from 900 to 1200 and built the fortress of Sacsayhuamán about 1100
facts.where: In the central Andes of south-eastern Peru, at about 3,400 metres, between the Huatanay and Urubamba rivers, near the Sacred Valley
facts.known: Capital of the Inca Empire; the Qurikancha, the Temple of the Sun; Sacsayhuamán; Inca stonework used as the base of the Spanish city; the siege of 1536; the Cusco School of painting; earthquakes; the Inti Raymi festival
facts.today: Cusco is the capital of the Cusco Province and Department of Peru, an archbishopric, and a World Heritage Site since 1983.

t: Cusco was occupied by the Killke people from about 900, became the capital of the Kingdom of Cusco and then of the Inca Empire, and was planned round two channelled rivers, four quarters and roads to the four provinces.
The Spanish entered the city in November 1533, plundered its palaces and temples and built a new city on Inca walls; Manco Inca besieged it for ten months in 1536 and failed.
Earthquakes in 1650 and 1950 destroyed much of the colonial city, and the Inca walls that withstood them are now visible again.
dyk: When the earthquake of 1950 damaged more than a third of the city's structures, Inca architecture withstood it, and the damage exposed granite retaining walls of the Qurikancha that had been hidden.
ev: The Killke build the walled complex of Sacsayhuamán

sections.origins:
The Quechua name of the city is Qusqu. Although it was used in Southern Quechua, the name is traced to the Aymara phrase qusqu wanka, "rock of the owl", which is tied to the foundation myth of the Ayar siblings. In one account of the myth, Ayar Awqa (Ayar Auca) was turned into a rock to mark his lineage's possession of the land, and Manco Capac and his companion, with four women, built a house and planted maize taken from the cave called Pacaritambo, "those of origin". The Spanish adopted the local name and wrote it Cuzco or, less often, Cozco; the form Cusco was also used in colonial times.

The city stands in the central Andes between the Huatanay and Urubamba rivers, at around 3,400 metres, with the Vilcabamba range to the north. The Killke people occupied the region from 900 to 1200 CE, before the Inca arrived in the 13th century. Carbon-14 dating of Saksaywaman, the walled complex outside Cusco, shows that the Killke built it about 1100. In March 2008 archaeologists found the ruins of a temple, a roadway and an aqueduct system there, with 11 rooms thought to have held idols and mummies. By tradition the city was founded by Manco Cápac as the capital of the Kingdom of Cusco, in the 12th century by one dating.
sections.growth:
Inca legend credits Sapa Inca Pachacuti with rebuilding Cusco and turning the Kingdom of Cusco from a sleepy city-state into the empire of Tawantinsuyu. Archaeological evidence, however, points to a slower, more organic growth that began before Pachacuti. The city was built to a definite plan, with two rivers channelled around it, and archaeologists have suggested that the plan was repeated at other sites. Many believe that Cusco was laid out as the effigy of a puma, a sacred animal. How it was built, and how its large stones were quarried and moved, remain undetermined. Its streets followed the orientation of the sun, and its builders kept to the shape of the land.

Under the Inca the city had two sectors, hurin and hanan, which together covered the four provinces of Chinchasuyu, Antisuyu, Kuntisuyu and Qullasuyu; a road led from each quarter of the city to the matching quarter of the empire. Each local leader had to build a house in Cusco and live there part of the year, in the quarter matching the one where he held territory. After Pachacuti, an Inca's title passed to one son and his property to a corporation of his other relatives, so each new title holder had to build a new house and add new lands. The Qurikancha, "golden place", was the chief sanctuary of the Sun god Inti, and Sacsayhuamán was expanded by the Inca.
sections.rulers:
Cusco was the capital of the Inca Empire, which is dated from the 13th century to 1532, and before that of the Kingdom of Cusco. After the death of Huayna Capac in 1528 the city fell to the sphere of Huáscar in the Inca civil war. Generals of Atahualpa captured it in April 1532 at the Battle of Quipaipan. The first three Spaniards arrived in May 1533, after the Battle of Cajamarca, to collect gold for Atahualpa's ransom. Francisco Pizarro officially arrived on 15 November 1533 and gave Manco Inca the Inca fringe as the new leader. Alcaldes and regidores were named on 24 March 1534, among them Gonzalo and Juan Pizarro, and the city was re-established on 23 March 1534. Pizarro left a garrison of 90 men.

Pizarro chose Lima as the capital of the new territories because it was close to the sea, and Cusco lost prominence, though it was the first city of the viceroyalty to have a bishop. It was later the capital of a corregimiento, of the Intendancy of Cusco and, towards the end of the viceroyalty, of the Royal Audiencia of Cusco. Independence was declared in 1821, but Cusco kept its loyalty to the King of Spain until 1824 and was the last colonial capital, under Viceroy José de la Serna. After the defeat at Ayacucho was known, the city council accepted the capitulation on 22 December 1824 and recognised Agustín Gamarra as prefect; patriot troops entered on 25 December. Cusco has always been the capital of its department.
sections.life:
Cusco was long an important centre of the indigenous peoples, and the Quechua people still live in the city. Spanish observers wrote that the capital astonished them by the length and regularity of its streets, that the great square was surrounded by palaces, and that in delicacy of stonework the natives far excelled the Spaniards. Under Spanish rule it was the centre of colonial rule and of the spread of Christianity in the Andean world, and it prospered from agriculture, cattle raising, mining and trade with Spain. The Spanish built churches, convents, a cathedral, a university and an archdiocese. Bishop Vicente de Valverde built his cathedral facing the plaza.

The colonial city grew on Inca foundations. The first cathedral, the Iglesia del Triunfo, was built in 1539 on the foundations of the palace of Viracocha Inca; the main cathedral, built between 1560 and 1664, used red granite blocks taken from Saksaywaman. The Jesuit church, begun in 1576, stands on the site of the Amarucancha, the palace of Wayna Qhapaq, and San Blas has the oldest parish church in Cusco, built in 1563. The street Hatun Rumiyuq, "the one with the big stone", holds the Stone of Twelve Angles and the palace of Inca Roca, later the Archbishop's residence. The city developed the Cuzco School of painting. Catholicism is the most common religion, the Inca religion is also practised by the Quechua people, and Inti Raymi is held on 24 June at Sacsayhuamán.
sections.crises:
The Spanish plundered the palaces and religious buildings, including the royal mummies in the Coricancha, and destroyed many Inca buildings, temples and palaces, using the remaining walls as the bases of a new city. Pizarro is said to have sacked much of the Inca city in 1535. The Qurikancha was destroyed, and the Convent of Santo Domingo was built on it. In the siege of 1536 Manco Inca Yupanqui took control of the city from the Spanish. The siege lasted ten months and failed; his forces held the city for only a few days. He withdrew to Vilcabamba, capital of the small Neo-Inca State, which survived another 36 years, and he never returned. Many Incas died in smallpox epidemics, having no acquired immunity.

In 1650 a violent earthquake destroyed almost all the colonial buildings, and the effigy of the Lord of the Earthquakes, still carried in procession each year, gained great importance. In 1781 the army of Túpac Amaru II besieged the city during the rebellion against the Bourbon Reforms. He was taken prisoner and executed with his entire family in the Plaza de Armas, though the rebellion went on until 1783. The Cuzco Rebellion of 1814 was put down in less than a year. A second earthquake on 21 May 1950 damaged more than a third of the city's structures; another had struck nine years earlier. A decline in the 19th century is tied to the emigration of Spanish families and the loss of trade, and the population was 47,000 in the 1840s.
sections.legacy:
Cusco was built on layers of cultures: Inca buildings stood on Killke structures, and Spanish churches and mansions replaced Inca temples and palaces. Much of the Inca masonry is visible today. After the 1950 earthquake the granite retaining walls of the Qurikancha were exposed, and restoration at the Santo Domingo complex uncovered Inca masonry without damaging the colonial building. The Cuzco School of painting is the first school established in Peru and in the Americas, and its pictures fill the cathedral and the Jesuit church, among them a Last Supper in which Jesus and the apostles eat guinea pig. The Quechua festival Inti Raymi continues on the esplanade of Sacsayhuamán.

The city's spelling is not fixed: in 1976 the mayor ordered the spelling Cusco in municipal publications, and in 1990 local authorities adopted Qosqo, which later administrations did not follow. The Constitution of Peru of 1993 names Cusco the Historical Capital of Peru, and UNESCO declared it a World Heritage Site in 1983. It is the capital of the Cusco Province and Department, the seat of an archbishop, and the base for visiting Inca sites such as Ollantaytambo and Machu Picchu. Several hundred thousand people live in the city today.

summary: Cusco is a city in the Peruvian Andes where the Killke people built Sacsayhuamán about 1100 and the Inca placed their capital. The Spanish entered it in 1533 and built a new city on Inca walls, and earthquakes in 1650 and 1950 uncovered those walls again.
notes: Dates of the Spanish city: the introduction says the city was 're-established on 23 March 1534', the conquest section says alcaldes and regidores were named on 24 March 1534. Both given as the article gives them.

The article says Pizarro 'sacked much of the Inca city in 1535' (Main sites) but the conquest section places the plundering at the Spanish entry in November 1533. Not reconciled; the text says the dates do not match. The article gives no figures for the dead of the conquest or the 1536 siege, and no number of Spanish or Inca forces beyond the 90-man garrison.

Founding: the introduction says the city was founded in the 12th century by Manco Cápac; the Inca period section dates the empire from the 13th century and says the Inca arrived in the 13th century (and Inca legend credits Pachacuti with rebuilding). start 1100 is marked circa and is the earliest date: the Killke Sacsayhuamán about 1100, and the 12th-century founding. Killke dates are 'the 10th century' in the introduction and 900 to 1200 in the Killke section.

The article says the Inca civil war began 'after the death of Huayna Capac in 1528' and that Atahualpa's generals took Cusco in April 1532, then that Spanish explorers invaded 'nineteen months later' after 'kidnapping and murdering Atahualpa'; I wrote only the dates and kept 'Spanish entered' as 15 November 1533. Atahualpa's capture and death are not dated in the article.

The article says Manco Inca 'a leader of the Sapa Inca' and later Manco Inca Yupanqui; I wrote Manco Inca. It says he was given the Inca fringe by Pizarro; the siege was in 1536 and lasted ten months, his forces holding the city 'for only a few days'.
The Plaza de Armas is described as the 'Square of the warrior' in Inca times; left out. The Inca effigy-of-a-puma claim is hedged ('many believe'), as in the text.

Quechua names are as the article spells them: Qusqu, Qosqo, Qurikancha, Coricancha, Saksaywaman and Sacsayhuamán (both appear), Wayna Qhapaq and Huayna Capac, Tuq'ukachi (not used). I used Qurikancha and Sacsayhuamán in my own sentences and the article's spelling inside quoted or tied phrases.

Left out as present-day or guide material: tourism and its figures, climate, flag, coat of arms, anthem, sport, cinema, media, transport, healthcare, cuisine, politics of recent decades, the 2022 to 2023 protests, the COVID-19 pandemic. The 2017 population of 428,450 and the Cusco District figure are given with the year.

Facts wanted but not found: when Cusco was first settled and by whom beyond the legend; the Inca population; how the Spanish conquest and sack was carried out, casualties; the date and course of the city's decline in the 19th century (the article gives only the 1840s population of 47,000); the earthquake dates apart from 1650 and 1950 (the article says only that another earthquake came 'nine years previously' to 1950); the date of the university and archdiocese; the first Spanish bishop's name beyond Valverde.

The 19th-century decline is told from the article's own explanation (migration of Spanish families to Lima and Arequipa after the 1781 rebellion, and the commercial loss from the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata); the article gives no earlier population.
